messages.subject: Detection function selection by AIC vs. QQ / goodness of fit tests
messages.subject_clean: Detection function selection by AIC vs. QQ / goodness of fit tests
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all of you for making Distance and the associated R packages freely available and for advising us on their use. I'm hoping you can advise me on a model selection problem that probably comes up frequently but that I have not seen discussed before. (Please redirect me if it has.)

In the process of fitting many detection functions for marine mammal surveys I have noticed that occasionally the model with the lowest AIC does not have the best looking QQ plot or score the lowest Kolmogorov–Smirnov and/or Cramer-von Mises test. Could you please explain a bit how this can happen and what process you would use to select between models in this case?

Here is a concrete example to consider. Using the latest version of the R mrds package available on github, I fitted four detection functions for pilot whales observed from shipboard surveys off the U.S. Atlantic coast:

+-----+-----------------+-----------+---------+----------+----------+------+-------+-------+
| Key | Covariates      | Delta AIC |     AIC | K-S Test | CvM Test | ESHW | N Est |    CV |
+-----+-----------------+-----------+---------+----------+----------+------+-------+-------+
| hr  | GroupSize, Vis2 |      0.00 | 2412.22 |    0.059 |    0.051 | 1417 | 684.7 | 0.231 |
| hr  | GroupSize       |      0.07 | 2412.29 |    0.045 |    0.035 | 1291 | 663.4 | 0.212 |
| hr  | Vis2            |      4.37 | 2416.59 |    0.052 |    0.034 | 1387 | 629.6 | 0.225 |
| hr  |                 |      5.50 | 2417.72 |    0.041 |    0.020 | 1224 | 604.4 | 0.203 |
+-----+-----------------+-----------+---------+----------+----------+------+-------+-------+

There were 148 sightings in these models. I truncated a relatively modest number out of a desire to preserve as many observations as possible for a subsequent density surface model. I attached detection function and QQ plots and summary .txt files for these four models.

GroupSize is the number of animals in the group; this was provided as the size column of the R data frame, but is called GroupSize in most of my documentation here. Vis2 is a subjective assessment of "visibility", essentially how far observers could see given weather and other conditions at the time. Low numbers mean better visibility. I attached plots showing the distribution of these data. The covariates behave in the expected way: sightings of large groups or during better visibility are easier to detect at distance.

As you can see, the model with the lowest AIC had the highest K-S Test, CvM Test, and CV, while the one with the highest AIC scored the lowest on those statistics. I presume the models that included covariates were penalized in AIC for including those parameters; despite this, they still scored lowest. (Admittedly, a delta AIC of 0.07 is certainly not much.)

Thanks for any advice you can provide. I am working on several large studies that will have likely at least 100 detection functions between them. I will not be able to spend endless time optimizing each one and must take a systematic approach to complete this in a reasonable time. My current approach is to choose the model with the lowest AIC, after discarding models that score very poorly on other tests (yet sometimes result in extremely low AICs) or are otherwise obviously problematic.

Best,

Jason

messages.body_plain:
Jason

Interesting question, thanks for providing the details of your analysis.  Here are a handful of random thoughts on model selection, precision and inference.  Others may take a different view on these matters.

- To begin with, as you note, your example consists of models that all adequately explain the pattern in a decent data set.  From that foundation, things are going to go smoothly regardless of model selection decisions.  The fundamental reason most of us analyse distance sampling data is to estimate abundance--model selection is a means to an end, rather than an end to itself.

- Note the abundance estimates and measure of precision of your results.  The confidence interval half-width for the first model is roughly 270.  Hence the estimates are effectively the same for all models presented.

- Secondly, all models presented fit the data very very well.  The significance level of the goodness of fit test for the "poorest" fitting model is 0.7.  There is little reason to find models that fit better than adequately.  I would draw the same inference about pilot whale abundance whichever of the four models I used for my inference.

- Model selection is an art rather than a science.  There are biological/fieldwork reasons for making inference from models that do not have the lowest AIC; see work from my colleague Dr. Thomas
>
> Williams, R. and L. Thomas. 2007. Distribution and abundance of marine mammals in the coastal waters of British Columbia, Canada. Journal of Cetacean Research and Management 9: 15-28. (see Pacific white-sided dolphins)

- There has been a running discussion in the statistical literature suggesting that AIC may have a tendency to over-fit; selecting models with too many parameters--one could argue your example supports that contention.  My personal preference in modelling is to use a model that fits adequately (rather than really well); because I am trying to model the process that gives rise to the data observed, rather than trying to model the data (and their noise) exactly.

I appreciate your interest in automating the model selection process.  I would likely do something similar to what you have done.  First filter out models with goodness-of-fit P-values < something, then plot the detection function upon data histogram figure for the top ~4-5 models, then (unfortunately from an automation perspective) pass a human eyeball over the summary table and figure to make a final determination.

messages.body_plain:
Eric,

Thank you very much for your fast and thoughtful reply. I appreciate you sharing your general view of the detection model selection process and also your observations about my example models.

On one hand, it would be interesting to fully understand the statistical details behind why adding a covariate would both reduce AIC but increase the K-S test. Perhaps it results from model fitting taking a maximum likelihood approach while the K-S test looks at prediction error, or something like that, and optimizing for one does not always lead to the optimal result for the other.

On the other hand, groking those details would probably not help me automate detection model selection further. If you and Len Thomas still view it as art rather than science, I should probably continue treat it that way, too. At present, I do not see an automation approach that would allow me to blindly trust the result—otherwise I’m sure you guys would have implemented it already. I will focus on using automation to select a small number of candidates and then manually select one (using a consistent and systematic approach, if possible, across the many datasets and species I am investigating).

Thanks for the pointer to the 2007 article. I will look up that example and take it into consideration.

Best,

Jason

messages.subject: Problem with sightings rounded to distance zero
messages.subject_clean: Problem with sightings rounded to distance zero
messages.body_plain:
I have a situation in which I suspect sightings rounded to distance zero are leading to a sub-optimal detection function. In your opinion, is the problem severe enough in this particular situation (see below) to require attention, and what is the appropriate way to address it?

I have ~600 sightings of North Atlantic right whales sighted from a Twin Otter aircraft on surveys of the southeast U.S coast. The plane few at 1000 ft; position and altitude were logged with GPS every few seconds. There were two observers with bubble windows, allowing visibility of the trackline. From what I can tell, the survey protocol was designed and executed with distance sampling in mind. However, observers did not collect perpendicular distance measurements (e.g. with inclinometers). Instead, the aircraft broke from the trackline, overflew the sighted group and marked it with GPS.

Using trigonometry, I calculated perpendicular distance to that “actual position” from the trackline vector estimated from 30 seconds of position points logged up to the break to circle the sighting. 633 sightings remained after right truncation. A hazard rate detection function fitted to these showed a spike at the shortest distance bin and the QQ plot showed slight bias at close distances (see attached cds_hr.pdf and .txt). (There were also notably short bins at about 600 and 1500 meters, but I suspect these are random.)

On investigation, I found that 33 sightings had a distance of exactly zero. For these sightings, it appeared the survey team pressed the “actual position” button in their software before breaking from the trackline. In several cases they logged messages similar to “Whale surfaced directly under the plane!”

My suspicion is that in these “directly under the plane” events, most of the sightings were not exactly on the trackline but the team did not see a need to overfly the sighting again to collect a post-break “actual position”. As a consequence, the distances of these were all exactly zero, because the actual positions were logged while still exactly on the trackline.

As an experiment, I left truncated the data at a distance of 1 m and fitted the detection function again. 34 sightings were removed: the 33 at distance 0 and one more at distance 0.032 which is based on a post-break overflight. This removed the spike from the closest distance bin and the deviation from the diagonal on the QQ plot (see attached cds_hr_with_left_trunc.pdf and .txt). Goodness of fit statistics generally improved. But estimated abundance went down from 1332 (CV=0.052) to 1176 (CV=0.051).

What do you believe is the best thing to do in this case? Left truncation certainly improves the fit of the detection function but arguably results in an underestimation of abundance. The 33 sightings at distance zero should have been spread over a larger distance and then counted in the estimate. Instead they were discarded. The width of the survey remained essentially the same (smaller by 1 meter), so estimated density will be significantly less.

I suppose if I could plausibly estimate the range of distances those sightings were likely to be spread over, I could left truncate at that outermost distance, or try to smear the sightings somehow. But that seems complicated and I’m not really certain how to estimate that distance range.

Thanks for your thoughts,

Jason

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Problem with sightings rounded to distance zero
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Problem with sightings rounded to distance zero
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason, list,

The way I see it, Distance was able do do the right thing without the left truncation, i.e. it cut through the spike. That is not surprising, since the small number of parameters that the model includes would not be able to fit it any way. So the density estimate is probably reasonable, even if the GOF statistics say it's a bad fit. It is a bad fit, but you know why. I agree the other dips and spikes might just be spurious, even though with 633 sightings I would not really expect such strong patterns in some specific bands, as you say around 600 and 1500m, but the way you described the distances are obtained, can't think of another obvious explanation (unless there was some partially blind spot?). So possibly you really only have a problem in terms of GOF, but no real bias, so you could just simply ignore it.

Or, if you prefer not to do that, and get nicer looking detection function plots and GOF stats, you could also just bin the data. I suspect that if you bin the data into 250 m bins, which just assumes that all those 0's would be within 250 m from the line, which seems reasonable given your description of the physics involved, (I suspect) you will get a little loss of precision, if any, and a very similar estimate to that obtained with all the data...

Hope this helps, maybe others have additional thoughts (if you implement any of this let me know what happens  - possibly on the side if not relevant to the list)

Tiago

messages.subject: Calculating abundance estimates for small sites
messages.subject_clean: Calculating abundance estimates for small sites
messages.body_plain:
When calculating abundance, online tutorials/examples on using Distance tend to assume the aim is to extrapolate from multiple sites to a larger area. For my study, I want to compare between small sites, so I need values for each site.

I have collected point count data for birds at 45 sites of 1Ha each, each on four occasions (2X am; 2X pm) and I would like to calculate abundance of specific species for each of these small 45 sites, e.g. without extrapolating to a wider area.

I have calculated detection functions for each species (using data from all sites within one habitat type and following online tutorials/guidance).

Do you know of any worked examples that do a similar thing? Has anyone on here done a similar thing in the past, and would you be happy to advise me on how to do this?

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Calculating abundance estimates for small sites
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Calculating abundance estimates for small sites
messages.body_plain:
Charlotte

Thanks for looking through our online materials; we hope to expand those in the near future.

But regarding your question of point-specific abundance estimates.  This is tricky.  You note that you pool data across points (within habitat type) to produce your detection function.  This is probably because you do not have enough detections per point to produce point-specific detection functions.  By pooling across points you induce a dependence in abundance estimates between points; they share common information in their detection functions.  Consequently, comparisons between point-specific abundance estimates are not valid because of the induced dependency.

If you were in the enviable position of having sufficient detections per point to produce point-specific detection functions, then you would be able to produce independent point-specific abundance estimates and comparisons would be valid.

Given you have pooled within habitats, your halfway-house might be to make inferences on a habitat-specific basis.  I do not know if that is consistent with the objectives of your study, but that could be a way forward for you.

The message the Distance software is showing is simply a warning, not an
error.  The message is stating that usually the average observed group
size is larger than the adjusted group size; however for your dataset,
the average observed group size is smaller than the adjusted group
size.  The message suggests this is an unusual situation (but not an
error).  You should assess the situation and decide if it is reasonable
that in the field you are not failing to detect small groups at large
distances.

messages.subject: Applying fitted detection function to new data?
messages.subject_clean: Applying fitted detection function to new data?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

We're using distance sampling to estimate abundance of moose, with data gathered along line transects during aerial surveys. The population we're working with is small and sparsely distributed across a large geographic area. In previous years, aerial surveys generated too few detections to accurately model a detection function, so during this year's surveys we focused exclusively on acquiring enough detections to get a precise estimate of detection, including covariates, with the hopes of using this function as a robust model for application to future surveys. Fortunately, we acquired enough detections this year to test several covariates and ended up with a fitted detection function with a covariate on habitat type and a low coefficient of variation.

Is there a way, using Distance, to apply this detection function to new data? So, for example, if we wanted to estimate abundance in 2016 using last year's survey data, is there a way to use our fitted detection function from this year with last year's data? We have no reason to suspect that detection probabilities would change between years. We're using the most recent version of Distance in R.

Any help would be much appreciated.

Dear All,

I am trying to select a cut-off point for right truncation. My data is from line transects and I want to truncate my observations using more than simply a rule of thumb value (e.g., 10% or 15%) or visual observation of my pdf curve and data histogram.Someone suggest me to decide based on goodness of fit tests like Chi-square, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises for different percentages of data exclusion (0% to 20% of observations), but the models with the best fits are not always the ones with the lower coefficient of variation. For example, these are some of my models with greater fit p-values for Chi-square and K-S tests (in decreasing order):

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-o2tS2Q0bGpo/WS9P4COTznI/AAAAAAAAAEQ/tKGauKQTgmEXXfzshN3o5GK6dlxmY3kGACLcB/s1600/models_fit.png>

Here by excluding 9% of observations (first in the list) I get the greater fit (larger p-values for Chi-square GOF and K-S GOF), but the CV is larger than a model with relatively poorer fit, excluding 6% of the data (fourth model in this list). So, in this case what is the best option to choose a right truncation cut off point?

As additional information, distances of all my observations were calculated using a rangefinder and I let the program to select the distance intervals for the histogram . When distances are measured accurately, it is always a good option to let the program define the distance intervals or it is still better to define them manually? This is another doubt I have but also connected as fit is affected with this decision.

Thanks in advance for any clarification on this matter, or any suggestions.

MSc. Sergio Nolazco
Institute of Biosciences
University of Sao Paulo
Brazil
